title: Influence of AI-driven Inquiry Teaching on Learning Outcomes
venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-driven inquiry teaching is associated with improved learning outcomes in higher education. The study frames AI as a support for organizing inquiry activities rather than as the curriculum topic itself, and it breaks inquiry teaching into four components: questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary. The author investigates how each component relates to students’ learning outcomes and whether students’ familiarity with AI changes those outcomes.

The intervention/approach is not an implemented classroom experiment with a treatment group; instead, it is a questionnaire-based analysis of students’ perceptions of AI-driven inquiry teaching. The questionnaire was built from prior inquiry-learning instruments and administered to civil aviation students from six universities in China. The sample included 308 valid responses from college students across multiple grades and majors, and the paper reports Cronbach’s alpha, KMO/Bartlett tests, linear regression, and ANOVA.

The study concludes that all four inquiry-teaching components are positively associated with learning outcomes, with explanation focusing showing the strongest statistical effect. It also finds that students with greater familiarity with AI report higher learning outcomes in AI-driven inquiry teaching. Overall, the paper argues that AI can support inquiry pedagogy by helping teachers organize questioning, evidence gathering, explanation, and evaluation, but the evidence is correlational and based on self-reported survey data from a civil aviation context.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational survey study using a questionnaire, reliability/validity checks, and regression/ANOVA, but not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. The claims are based on self-reported perceptions rather than objective achievement measures, so causal credibility is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are statistically significant and positive, but the practical magnitude is unclear because the paper does not provide standard effect sizes and relies on survey data. The findings suggest modest, context-specific benefits in a college civil aviation sample rather than clearly demonstrated generalizable impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-driven inquiry teaching in a civil aviation higher-education context, structured around AI-supported questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary within inquiry lessons.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that AI-driven inquiry teaching was positively associated with learning outcomes, with the four inquiry components of questioning, evidence acquisition, explanation focusing, and evaluation summary showing estimated improvements of 10%, 5%, 1%, and 10%, respectively. The outcome was measured via a 4-item learning-outcome questionnaire in a survey of n=308 valid civil aviation students, and the overall model was significant (F(4,303)=13.061, p=0.000) with adjusted R2=0.936.
finding.measure: Learning outcome questionnaire (Likert-scale survey); regression analysis of AI-driven inquiry components

finding.finding_summary: Students' familiarity with AI was significantly related to learning outcomes, with relatively familiar students reporting higher mean scores than very unfamiliar students (4.52 ± 0.42 vs. 3.95 ± 0.86). The one-way ANOVA found a significant group effect (F=2.682, p=0.032) across five familiarity groups (n=308 valid responses), suggesting that comfort with AI may support engagement or confidence in AI-driven inquiry settings.
finding.measure: Learning outcome scores by self-reported familiarity with AI
